title: Calling and booking a table
goal: Make phone calls in Mandarin and say whether you've understood or not — through 聽得懂 and 聽不懂, the forms beginners need most.
bekal: make a call, book a table, and leave a message
use result complements (看到, 聽懂, 買到) and their potential forms
ask the other person to slow down or repeat

dialogs.title: 對話 — 訂位
dialogs.intro: Budi calls a restaurant to book a table for five. It's his first phone call in Mandarin.

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.id: Hello, good afternoon, Xiao Lin Restaurant.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Hello, I'd like to book a table.

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.text: [好的|Hǎo de]，[請問|qǐngwèn][幾位|jǐ wèi]？[什麼|Shénme][時候|shíhòu]？
lines.id: Sure, for how many people? And when?
lines.literal: good — (one), please — ask — how-many — (measure word)? what — time?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [五位|Wǔ wèi]，[明天|míngtiān][晚上|wǎnshang][七點|qī diǎn]。
lines.id: Five people, tomorrow evening at seven.
lines.literal: five — (measure word), tomorrow — evening — seven — o'clock.

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.text: [不好意思|Bù hǎoyìsi]，[七點|qī diǎn][客滿|kèmǎn][了|le]。[六點|Liù diǎn][半|bàn][可以|kěyǐ][嗎|ma]？
lines.id: Sorry, seven is fully booked. Is six thirty OK?
lines.literal: not — good — meaning, seven — o'clock — guest-full — (change). six — o'clock — half — can — (question)?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [不好意思|Bù hǎoyìsi]，[我|wǒ][沒|méi][聽|tīng][懂|dǒng]。[可以|Kěyǐ][說|shuō][慢|màn][一點|yìdiǎn][嗎|ma]？
lines.id: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you speak more slowly?
lines.literal: sorry, I — not — listen — understand. can — speak — slow — a-bit — (question)?

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.text: [沒|Méi][問題|wèntí]。[七|Qī]…[點|diǎn]…[滿|mǎn][了|le]。[六|Liù][點|diǎn][半|bàn]…[可以|kěyǐ]。
lines.id: No problem. Seven… o'clock… is full. Six thirty… is OK.
lines.literal: not — have — problem. seven… o'clock… full — (change). six — o'clock — half… can.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [啊|A]，[我|wǒ][聽|tīng][懂|dǒng][了|le]！[六點|Liù diǎn][半|bàn][沒|méi][問題|wèntí]。
lines.id: Ah, got it! Six thirty is no problem.
lines.literal: ah, I — listen — understand — (change)! six — o'clock — half — not — have — problem.

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.text: [請問|Qǐngwèn][怎麼|zěnme][稱呼|chēnghū]？[電話|Diànhuà][幾號|jǐ hào]？
lines.id: May I have your name? And your phone number?
lines.literal: please — ask — how — address? phone — what — number?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [我|Wǒ][姓|xìng][布|Bù]。[電話|Diànhuà][是|shì][0912-345-678|líng jiǔ yāo èr sān sì wǔ liù qī bā]。
lines.id: My surname is Bu. My number is 0912-345-678.

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.text: [好|Hǎo]，[布|Bù][先生|xiānshēng]，[五位|wǔ wèi]，[明天|míngtiān][六點|liù diǎn][半|bàn]。
lines.id: All right, Mr. Bu, five people, tomorrow at six thirty.
lines.literal: good, Bu — mister, five — (measure word), tomorrow — six — o'clock — half.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [對|Duì]。[請問|Qǐngwèn][有|yǒu][素食|sùshí][嗎|ma]？[我|Wǒ][朋友|péngyǒu][吃素|chīsù]。
lines.id: Right. May I ask, do you have vegetarian dishes? My friend is vegetarian.
lines.literal: right. please — ask — have — vegetable-food — (question)? I — friend — eat-vegetarian.

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.id: We do! We have three kinds of vegetarian dishes.
lines.literal: have — (softener)! we — have — three — kind — vegetable-food.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [太好了|Tài hǎo le]！[謝謝|Xièxie]，[明天|míngtiān][見|jiàn]！
lines.id: Great! Thank you, see you tomorrow!

notes: ⚠️ **The number 1 is read 幺 (*yāo*), not 一 (*yī*), in phone numbers and room numbers.** The reason is practical: *yī* sounds too much like *qī* (seven) over the phone. It's a rule rarely taught but used every day.
**怎麼稱呼？ ("how should I address you?") is the polite way to ask someone's name** on the phone and in formal settings. Your surname is enough as an answer: *我姓布*.
**客滿 ("guests full") means fully booked.** You'll see it on the doors of popular restaurants, especially on weekends. ⚠️ Famous restaurants in Taiwan often have to be booked weeks in advance.

**Phoning in a foreign language is much harder than talking face to face**, because there are no lip movements or gestures to help. ⚠️ Don't lose heart if your first call is a mess; write out your sentences before you dial.
**種 (*zhǒng*, kind) is the measure word for kinds or varieties**: 三種素食 (three kinds of vegetarian dishes), 兩種語言 (two languages).

grammars.title: Result complements: verbs that state their outcome
body: Mandarin often separates the **action** from its **result**. 看 means "look" (the action); to say you actually **saw** it, you add the result: 看**到**. English "look" vs "see" is a similar split — but Mandarin does it with almost every verb, and that's where beginners lose half the meaning.
after: ⚠️ **我看了 and 我看到了 are very different.** The first means "I looked/watched" (the action was done); the second means "I saw it" (the result was achieved). *我找了* = I looked for it; *我找到了* = I found it.
**Negate with 沒, and the whole complement stays**: *我沒聽懂* (I didn't catch it), *我沒買到* (I couldn't get one).
**吃飽了嗎？ is a very common greeting in Taiwan** — a friendly "have you eaten?" that works like "how are you?". Answer *吃飽了，謝謝*.

grammars.title: 得 and 不: can or can't reach the result
body: Insert **得** between the verb and its result to mean "can"; insert **不** to mean "can't". This form is used constantly and is extremely useful for beginners.
after: ⚠️ **聽不懂 is the most important phrase in this unit.** It means "I can't catch what you're saying" — not "I'm deaf" and not "I'm stupid". Say it without embarrassment; Taiwanese people will slow down right away.
**Tell 我不懂 apart from 我聽不懂.** The first means "I don't understand the idea"; the second means "my ears didn't catch the words". For beginners, the second is almost always the right one.
**來不及 ("not in time") is used all the time**: *快一點，來不及了！* ("hurry up, we'll be late!").

blocks.text: ⚠️ **打電話 ("hit the phone") means to make a call** — 打 is used for many activities that have nothing to do with hitting: 打電話, 打字 (type), 打球 (play ball), 打工 (work part-time), 打折 (give a discount). It's one of the most versatile verbs in Mandarin.

sections.title: Lifesaver phrases when you don't understand

blocks.title: Memorize all five today
items: **我聽不懂。** *Wǒ tīng bù dǒng.* — I don't understand (what you said).
**請說慢一點。** *Qǐng shuō màn yìdiǎn.* — Please speak more slowly.
**請再說一次。** *Qǐng zài shuō yí cì.* — Please say it again.
**可以寫下來嗎？** *Kěyǐ xiě xiàlái ma?* — Could you write it down?
**…是什麼意思？** *… shì shénme yìsi?* — What does … mean?

blocks.text: ⚠️ **These five phrases are worth more than two hundred words of vocabulary.** As long as you can say them, any conversation can be rescued — and Taiwanese people are almost always happy to slow down. What kills a conversation isn't what you don't know; it's silence.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Taiwanese phone numbers are read digit by digit, and 1 is read 幺 (*yāo*).** Mobile numbers always start with 09, so 0912-345-678 is read *líng jiǔ yāo èr — sān sì wǔ — liù qī bā*. Practice reading your own number until it's smooth; you'll be asked for it again and again.
